title: The DESI Data Release 1 white dwarf catalogue
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. Catalogue file available at https://cygnus.astro.warwick.ac.uk/phsdaj/WhiteDwarfs/Tables/DESI_DR1_catalogue_1.0.csv.gz
summary: The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument is conducting a redshift survey, mapping the universe in three dimensions to measure the history of cosmic expansion. As well as extragalactic objects, it is targeting millions of Milky Way stars, including white dwarfs. Using Data Release 1 we assemble the largest catalogue of spectroscopically-confirmed white dwarfs to date, whose straightforward selection function enables statistically-robust population studies. We visually inspect and fit models to spectra of 63968 objects, finding 44409 white dwarfs. We present their spectral classifications, atmospheric parameters and radial velocities. We assess survey completeness and uniformity, identify potential spectral contamination caused by flux from nearby sources entering the fibre, and assign confidence scores to our classifications to facilitate selection of statistical and observational samples. We present spectra representing most white dwarf classes, common and exotic. We conclude with recommendations and warnings regarding the use of the catalogue.

AI.tldr: Using DESI Data Release 1, the authors construct the largest catalogue of spectroscopically-confirmed white dwarfs to date, comprising 44,409 objects from 63,968 candidate spectra, with spectral classifications, atmospheric parameters, radial velocities, completeness assessments, and confidence scores for statistically robust population studies.
AI.motivation: To exploit DESI's capability of observing millions of Milky Way stars alongside extragalactic targets, producing a large, well-characterised white dwarf catalogue with a straightforward selection function that enables statistically rigorous population studies.
AI.method: Visual inspection and spectral model fitting of 63,968 objects from DESI Data Release 1; determination of spectral classifications, atmospheric parameters, and radial velocities; assessment of survey completeness and uniformity; identification of spectral contamination from nearby source flux in fibres; assignment of confidence scores to classifications.
AI.result: A catalogue of 44,409 spectroscopically-confirmed white dwarfs is presented, covering most white dwarf classes (common and exotic), with contamination assessment, completeness metrics, and confidence scoring to support selection of statistical and observational samples.
AI.conclusion: The DESI DR1 white dwarf catalogue represents the largest such sample to date; the authors provide recommendations and warnings regarding its use for future population studies and observational follow-up.

title: Improvements to Asteroseismic Fitting of White Dwarfs in the Gaia Era
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal. 20 pages, 13 figures
summary: White dwarf asteroseismology aims to constrain the interior structures of pulsating white dwarf stars by fitting observed pulsation periods to those computed for stellar models. However, there remain several obstacles for achieving reliable results with the model grid-fitting approach. We simulate data for a parameter recovery experiment in one and two dimensions (mass and effective temperature) to demonstrate improved methodologies that address challenges for characterizing degenerate asteroseismic solutions. We show that interpolating model periods onto a finer grid can adequately resolve asteroseismic solutions that would be missed with sparse model grids. Incorporating absolute magnitude from Gaia astrometry into the statistical fitting is shown to reduce solution degeneracy. We define a seismic solution as a solution to the mode identification problem, and we show that fitting to consistent model pulsation modes can isolate each candidate solution in degenerate solution space. A criterion based on $χ^2$ for what should be considered a reasonable fit is adopted, and we identify all combinations of model periods that meet this criterion, not only those nearest to the measured periods. Finally, we demonstrate how fitting Gaussians to probability distributions allows for the robust characterization of each candidate solution, including uncertainties. Our accurate characterization of the degenerate solution landscape is supported by the comparison of our solutions to a direct marginalization of the likelihood function. These fitting approaches can be generalized to higher dimensions, where there are more than two free parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper presents improved statistical methodologies for white dwarf asteroseismology, demonstrating in 1D and 2D parameter recovery experiments how model grid interpolation, incorporation of Gaia absolute magnitudes, consistent mode identification, χ²-based fit criteria, and Gaussian fitting to probability distributions collectively enable robust characterization of degenerate asteroseismic solutions.
AI.motivation: White dwarf asteroseismology aims to constrain stellar interior structures by fitting observed pulsation periods to model predictions, but the grid-fitting approach faces obstacles including sparse model grids missing solutions, degeneracy in solutions, and difficulty characterizing uncertainties.
AI.method: The authors perform parameter recovery experiments in one and two dimensions (mass and effective temperature) using simulated data. They interpolate model periods onto finer grids, incorporate Gaia absolute magnitude into statistical fitting, define seismic solutions via mode identification, apply a χ²-based criterion for acceptable fits, and fit Gaussians to probability distributions to characterize candidate solutions with uncertainties. Solutions are validated against direct likelihood marginalization.
AI.result: Interpolating model periods onto finer grids resolves asteroseismic solutions missed with sparse grids. Adding Gaia absolute magnitude reduces solution degeneracy. Consistent mode-fitting isolates each candidate solution in degenerate solution space. The χ² criterion identifies all reasonable model-period combinations, and Gaussian fitting to probability distributions robustly characterizes each solution with uncertainties. Results agree with direct likelihood marginalization.
AI.conclusion: These improved fitting methodologies enable accurate characterization of the degenerate solution landscape in white dwarf asteroseismology and generalize to higher-dimensional parameter spaces beyond mass and effective temperature.

title: Can isolated binaries form unequal-mass binary black-hole mergers with a high-spin primary black hole?
comment: submitted
summary: GWTC-5 has revealed a subpopulation of merging binary black holes (BBHs) with a high-spin primary black hole (BH) and possibly unequal BH masses. GW241110 additionally exhibits a large spin-orbit misalignment, which suggests a hierarchical-merger origin. However, other formation scenarios are possible or even likely, especially for events without constraints on spin-orbit misalignment. As an alternative to hierarchical mergers, we investigate whether binary evolution can produce unequal-mass BBH mergers with a high-spin primary BH. Rather than performing comprehensive population-synthesis calculations, we examine the evolutionary pathways of forming merging BBHs and assess their uncertainties. We identify two possible pathways for producing unequal-mass BBHs with a high-spin primary. In initially wide binaries, mass-ratio reversal can make the tidally spun-up second-born BH both more massive and more rapidly rotating than the first-born BH; alternatively, in an initially close, unequal-mass binary, the primary star may evolve chemically homogeneously, while the secondary star evolves normally, producing a high-spin first-born BH that is more massive than its companion. Generally, large spin-orbit misalignment can be produced by large natal kicks or tertiary-induced nodal precession and/or Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai oscillations. We conclude that hierarchical mergers are not uniquely required to produce unequal-mass BBHs with a high-spin primary BH, although each isolated-binary pathway faces important theoretical constraints. Future detections of more merger events with primary BH spins around 0.7 would discriminate between binary evolution and hierarchical merger origin.

AI.tldr: GWTC-5 and the event GW241110 revealed a subpopulation of merging binary black holes (BBHs) with high-spin primary black holes and possibly unequal masses. The paper investigates whether standard binary evolution (as an alternative to hierarchical mergers) can produce such systems, identifying two isolated-binary pathways: mass-ratio reversal in wide binaries producing a tidally spun-up second-born BH, and chemically homogeneous evolution in close, unequal-mass binaries producing a high-spin first-born BH. While large spin-orbit misalignments can arise from natal kicks or tertiary-induced precession/ZLK oscillations, each pathway faces theoretical constraints, and future detections of events with primary spin ~0.7 will discriminate between origins.
AI.motivation: Recent gravitational-wave observations (GWTC-5, GW241110) have revealed merging BBHs featuring high-spin primary black holes with possibly unequal masses and, in at least one case, large spin-orbit misalignment. While hierarchical mergers have been proposed as the origin, the authors aim to investigate whether standard isolated binary evolution can alternatively produce these systems, since hierarchical mergers may not be uniquely required.
AI.method: Instead of comprehensive population-synthesis calculations, the authors systematically examine the evolutionary pathways by which merging BBHs with a high-spin primary and unequal masses could form from isolated binaries, assessing the physical uncertainties and constraints associated with each pathway. Two candidate pathways are identified: (1) mass-ratio reversal in initially wide binaries where the tidally spun-up second-born BH becomes heavier and faster-rotating than the first-born BH, and (2) chemically homogeneous evolution of the primary in close, unequal-mass binaries while the secondary evolves normally. Mechanisms for producing large spin-orbit misalignment—natal kicks and tertiary-induced nodal precession and/or Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai oscillations—are also evaluated.
AI.result: The authors identify two possible isolated-binary pathways that can produce unequal-mass BBH mergers with a high-spin primary BH: mass-ratio reversal with tidal spin-up in wide binaries, and chemically homogeneous evolution of the primary star in close binaries. Large spin-orbit misalignment can be generated via large natal kicks or third-body effects (nodal precession and/or ZLK oscillations). However, each pathway faces significant theoretical uncertainties and constraints. The authors conclude that hierarchical mergers are not uniquely required to explain these systems, and predict that future detections of merger events with primary BH spin around 0.7 would help discriminate between binary evolution and hierarchical merger origins.
AI.conclusion: Isolated binary evolution can plausibly produce unequal-mass BBHs with high-spin primary black holes, so hierarchical mergers are not uniquely required to explain the GWTC-5/GW241110 observations. However, each identified pathway is subject to important theoretical constraints. Differentiating between formation channels will require further gravitational-wave detections with primary BH spins around 0.7 to statistically discriminate binary-evolution from hierarchical-merger origins.

title: Energy Partitioning at the Termination Shock
summary: We show new results of a global 3D magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation of the Boston University outer heliosphere model where we used a newly developed approach that distributes the non-adiabatic shock heating among the cold protons, electrons, and pickup-ions (PUIs), while maintaining total energy conservation of all ions (cold protons and PUIs) and electrons. In our previous simulations ( E.S. Bair et al. 2025; B. van der Holst et al. 2026), all non-adiabatic shock heating was channeled to the cold protons, resulting in a too large temperature jump at the termination shock (TS) for the thermal solar wind. Using a new methodology we improved the simulation results with respect to the temperature jump observed at the TS by Voyager 2 (V2) spacecraft. Our simulations approached the observed jump conditions of a factor 10--20 in the cold solar wind temperature V2 measurements, and we obtain improvements in the simulation results relative to the data. Because we directly estimate in this way the distribution of non-adiabatic heating at the TS, we have the opportunity to study the physical process of heating cold plasma and PUIs in the TS. The results show that having almost 100\% non-adiabatic shock heating going towards PUIs at the TS reproduces the jump conditions observed along the V2 trajectory. This information is key to understanding the physical processes that shape the heliosphere. As shown by M. Opher et al. (2020), PUIs significantly change the shape of the heliosphere, for example, the presence of hot PUIs results in a deflated inner heliosheath. Our work provides the architecture of how energy partitioning at shocks in kinetic simulations (J. Giacalone et al. 2021) can be utilized in global MHD models.

AI.tldr: This paper presents improvements to the Boston University outer heliosphere global MHD simulation by developing a new approach that distributes non-adiabatic shock heating among cold protons, electrons, and pickup ions (PUIs) while conserving total energy. Unlike previous simulations where all shock heating went to cold protons (causing overly large temperature jumps at the termination shock), this method allocates nearly 100% of non-adiabatic heating to PUIs, successfully reproducing the factor 10–20 temperature jump observed by Voyager 2. This work bridges kinetic simulation energy partitioning to global MHD models and provides insight into heliosphere structure.
AI.motivation: Previous global MHD simulations of the outer heliosphere channeled all non-adiabatic shock heating to cold protons, producing temperature jumps at the termination shock that were too large compared to Voyager 2 observations. The authors seek to correct this discrepancy by properly partitioning shock heating among the different ion populations and electrons, which is essential for accurately modeling the physical processes that shape the heliosphere.
AI.method: A new energy partitioning methodology was developed for the Boston University model. The approach distributes non-adiabatic shock heating among cold protons, electrons, and pickup ions (PUIs) while strictly maintaining total energy conservation across all ions and electrons. This effectively transfers energy partitioning insights from kinetic simulations (e.g., Giacalone et al. 2021) into the global MHD framework.
AI.result: The new method successfully reproduces the observed temperature jump of a factor 10–20 at the termination shock along the Voyager 2 trajectory, significantly improving upon previous simulations. Notably, allocating nearly 100% of the non-adiabatic shock heating to pickup ions yields the jump conditions consistent with V2 measurements, demonstrating improved agreement with observational data.
AI.conclusion: The results indicate that pickup ions receive essentially all non-adiabatic heating at the termination shock, which is critical for understanding the physical processes shaping the heliosphere (including the deflated inner heliosheath caused by hot PUIs). This work demonstrates a viable architecture for incorporating shock energy partitioning from kinetic simulations into global MHD models, providing a framework for more accurate heliospheric simulations.

title: JWST/NIRSpec Reveals Diverse Nuclear Environments in Dwarf Galaxies Hosting AGN
comment: 27 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Accepted to ApJ
summary: Dwarf galaxies, in the $Λ$CDM framework, are expected to dominate the galaxy number density at all redshifts. As such, studying AGN in these systems, including characterizing their local environments and emission properties, is essential in obtaining a comprehensive view of the AGN population and their influence on their host galaxy. To this end, we present JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations of four dwarf galaxies (M$_\star<$10$^{9.5}\;$M$_\odot$) with evidence of AGN activity. Utilizing the improvements in resolution and sensitivity offered by JWST, we investigate the emission features of the central kiloparsec of these dwarfs. Our findings include the detection of over 100 emission lines across our sample, including coronal lines with ionization potentials greater than 300 eV. The nuclear spectra show diverse emission features. In two galaxies, we measure strong contributions from hot dust to the infrared continuum. We also detect both PAH and coronal line emission within 100 parsecs of the nuclei in three galaxies. We estimate the hot H$_2$ gas mass to be between 1--20 M$_\odot$ within 300 pc across our sample, where both thermal and non-thermal excitation are involved. Lastly, spatial flux maps reveal varied emission structures across all observed gas phases, ranging from radial symmetry around the nucleus to elongated plumes. Kinematic maps also show each galaxy has unique velocity structures despite all being isolated, affirming the diversity of rotation curves problem, a long standing tension between simulations and observations. These results showcase the unique and varied nuclear environments that can be found in dwarf galaxies hosting AGN.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations of four dwarf galaxies (M★<10^9.5 M⊙) with AGN activity reveal over 100 emission lines, coronal lines with ionization potentials >300 eV, hot dust contributions, PAH and coronal line emission within 100 pc of nuclei, hot H2 gas masses of 1-20 M⊙ within 300 pc, and diverse spatial/kinematic structures. The galaxies exhibit unique velocity structures despite being isolated, relevant to the diversity of rotation curves problem.
AI.motivation: Dwarf galaxies are expected to dominate galaxy number density at all redshifts in the ΛCDM framework, so studying AGN in these systems (their environments and emission properties) is essential for a comprehensive understanding of the AGN population and their impact on host galaxies.
AI.method: JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations of four dwarf galaxies (M★<10^9.5 M⊙) with AGN evidence, used to investigate emission features of the central kiloparsec. Analysis includes spectral line identification, measurement of coronal lines, hot dust continuum contributions, PAH detection, estimation of hot H2 gas mass via excitation mechanisms, and spatial flux/kinematic mapping across multiple gas phases.
AI.result: Detection of over 100 emission lines including coronal lines (>300 eV ionization potentials). Two galaxies show strong hot dust contributions to infrared continuum. Three galaxies exhibit PAH and coronal line emission within 100 pc of nuclei. Hot H2 gas masses range 1-20 M⊙ within 300 pc with both thermal and non-thermal excitation. Spatial flux maps reveal varied structures from radially symmetric to elongated plumes; kinematic maps show unique velocity structures per galaxy despite isolation, affirming the diversity of rotation curves problem.
AI.conclusion: The results showcase the unique and varied nuclear environments found in dwarf galaxies hosting AGN, contributing to our understanding of AGN properties in low-mass systems and highlighting tensions with simulations regarding rotation curve diversity.

title: ROCKETS I: Investigating the Impact of the Rocket Effect on Two Nearby Young Open Clusters Encased in Infrared Bubbles
comment: 13 Pages, 10 Figures, 1 Table, accepted for publication in Publications of the Astronomical Society of Australia
summary: We introduce ROCKETS (Rocket-driven Cluster Kinematics & Triggered Star-formation), a Gaia based programme investigating kinematic fingerprints of stellar feedback or rocket effect in young star forming regions. We analyse two young clusters with O-type stars enclosed by mid-infrared bubbles, Collinder 69 and IC 1396 as a methodological demonstration on two nearby benchmark regions. Co-moving candidates are selected within an astrometric ellipse defined by the median and median absolute deviation of Class I/II YSOs with Gaia data. For each star, we compute a relative proper-motion angle (RPMA) relative to the ionising source. In both regions the RPMA distribution shows a strong excess at RPMA $<15^{\circ}$, corresponding to sources moving away from the respective ionising sources. We quantify this using the Rocket Effect Index (REI), finding $\mathrm{REI}\simeq 1.1$ for Collinder 69 and $\mathrm{REI}\simeq 1.7$ for IC 1396. When considering only Class I/II YSOs, the REI of both regions increases to $\mathrm{REI}\gtrsim 10$. Velocity-structure analysis of the sample shows that the RPMA $<15^\circ$ subset has stronger positive pairwise expansion than the full co-moving population, providing additional support for the rocket effect. The outward-moving stars are not uniformly distributed; instead, their position angles are strongly anisotropic and preferentially aligned towards the bright-rimmed clouds. Gaia colour-magnitude diagrams show no strong age offset between sources moving outward and literature cluster members. The observed kinematic signatures support feedback-driven acceleration of gas and triggered star formation preferentially towards higher density regions of expanding bubbles due to the rocket effect.

AI.tldr: ROCKETS is a Gaia-based programme measuring the "rocket effect" (feedback-driven stellar acceleration) in two young star-forming regions with O-type stars, Collinder 69 and IC 1396. Using relative proper-motion angles (RPMA) and a Rocket Effect Index (REI), the authors find strong excess of sources moving away from the ionising stars (REI~1.1-1.7 for all co-moving sources, REI>10 for Class I/II YSOs), with outward-moving stars anisotropically aligned towards bright-rimmed clouds, supporting feedback-driven acceleration and triggered star formation.
AI.motivation: To investigate and quantify kinematic fingerprints of stellar feedback (the "rocket effect") in young star-forming regions using Gaia astrometry, testing whether feedback-driven acceleration removes or triggers star formation at expanding bubble edges, and establishing ROCKETS as a methodological framework.
AI.method: Selection of co-moving candidates within an astrometric ellipse defined by median and MAD of Class I/II YSOs with Gaia data. Computation of a relative proper-motion angle (RPMA) for each star relative to the ionising source. Quantification via the Rocket Effect Index (REI), along with velocity-structure analysis (pairwise expansion) and Gaia colour-magnitude diagrams for age comparison. Analysis of position-angle anisotropy relative to bright-rimmed clouds.
AI.result: Both regions show strong RPMA excess at <15 degrees (outward motion), with REI~1.1 (Collinder 69) and ~1.7 (IC 1396); REI rises above 10 when only Class I/II YSOs are considered. The outward-moving subset exhibits stronger positive pairwise expansion. Outward-moving stars are anisotropically distributed and preferentially aligned towards bright-rimmed clouds, with no significant age offset between outward movers and cluster members.
AI.conclusion: The observed kinematic signatures support the rocket effect as a mechanism of feedback-driven gas acceleration and triggered star formation preferentially towards higher-density regions of expanding bubbles around O-type stars.

title: Super-Eddington Accretion and Early-Stage Feedback in Ton S180
comment: 15 pages (main text), 8 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A (1 September 2026)
summary: Narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLSy1) galaxies are key laboratories for studying rapid supermassive black hole (SMBH) growth and active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback at high accretion rates. We investigate the nearby NLSy1 Ton S180 with VLT-MUSE optical integral field spectroscopy to connect its nuclear accretion properties with the spatially resolved ionized gas and host-galaxy kinematics. We modeled the unresolved nuclear spectrum and applied a custom point spread function subtraction to recover the host-galaxy emission on kiloparsec scales. The nuclear spectrum requires a complex permitted-line decomposition and a blueshifted [O III] outflow component. Single-epoch estimators and the stellar velocity dispersion imply black hole masses in the range $\log(M_{\rm BH}/M_\odot) = 6.5 - 7.7$. Combined with the observed luminosity, this implies a dimensionless mass accretion rate of $\dot{M} / \dot{M}_{\rm Edd} = 4.1 - 980$, confirming the extreme accretion regime. The host galaxy shows a circumnuclear ring, an inner elongated structure consistent with a bar, and rotation-dominated gas and stellar kinematics. Simple inflow models do not significantly better reproduce the observed velocity field. We detect a resolved ionized outflow extending about 2 kpc west of the nucleus, with mildly blueshifted velocities (with a maximum of $v_{\rm max} \sim 340$ km s$^{-1}$). Its mass outflow rate is only $\sim 4.2 \times 10^{-4}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, whereas the unresolved nuclear outflow reaches $v_{\rm max} \sim 1140$ km s$^{-1}$ and $\dot{M}_{\rm out} > 1.5\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. This contrast may reflect either weak ionized coupling from nuclear to galactic scales or different episodes of AGN activity over time. These results show that Ton S180 is undergoing rapid SMBH growth, while the observed ionized outflow remains confined to the inner few kiloparsecs and is weak on host-galaxy scales.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a VLT-MUSE integral field spectroscopic study of the nearby NLSy1 galaxy Ton S180, modeling its nuclear spectrum and subtracting the PSF to recover host-galaxy emission. The black hole mass is estimated at log(M_BH/M_sun) = 6.5–7.7 with an extreme dimensionless accretion rate of 4.1–980. The host shows a circumnuclear ring, bar-like structure, and rotation-dominated kinematics. A resolved ionized outflow extends ~2 kpc west with only 4.2×10^-4 M_sun/yr mass outflow rate, contrasting with a nuclear outflow reaching 1140 km/s and >1.5 M_sun/yr, indicating weak ionized coupling or separate AGN episodes.
AI.motivation: NLSy1 galaxies are crucial for understanding rapid supermassive black hole growth and AGN feedback at high accretion rates. Ton S180 provides an opportunity to connect nuclear accretion properties with spatially resolved ionized gas and host-galaxy kinematics in a nearby system.
AI.method: VLT-MUSE optical integral field spectroscopy of Ton S180. The unresolved nuclear spectrum was modeled with complex permitted-line decomposition and a blueshifted [O III] outflow component. A custom PSF subtraction recovered host-galaxy emission on kiloparsec scales. Black hole masses were estimated using single-epoch estimators and stellar velocity dispersion.
AI.result: Black hole mass log(M_BH/M_sun) = 6.5–7.7 and dimensionless accretion rate 4.1–980, confirming extreme accretion. Host galaxy shows a circumnuclear ring, an inner bar-like elongated structure, and rotation-dominated kinematics. A resolved ionized outflow extends ~2 kpc west with v_max ~340 km/s and mass outflow rate ~4.2×10^-4 M_sun/yr, while the unresolved nuclear outflow has v_max ~1140 km/s and M_dot_out > 1.5 M_sun/yr. Simple inflow models do not significantly improve the velocity field fit.
AI.conclusion: Ton S180 is undergoing rapid SMBH growth with extreme accretion, yet its ionized outflow is confined to the inner few kiloparsecs and weak on host-galaxy scales, suggesting either weak ionized coupling from nuclear to galactic scales or episodic AGN activity.

title: Metallicity dependence of Wolf-Rayet binaries using detailed binary models: An absence of long-period systems at low metallicity
comment: Submitted to A&A. Comments welcome
summary: Observations of Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars in binaries in the SMC and LMC suggest a preference for short period ($P\lesssim30$ days) orbits, with an apparent absence of WRs in long-period systems. The Galactic population does extend to longer periods but shows a deficit in long-period WR binaries compared to their progenitors, the O-star population. Across these populations a nearly constant binary fraction has been observed. We aim to characterize the population of WR binaries across a range of metallicity and determine the metallicity dependence of the formation of these systems, specifically focusing on the period distribution. We use detailed binary evolution models from POSYDON to predict the population of WR binaries at 0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.45, and $1Z_\odot$, analyzing the resulting period distribution and formation channels, while comparing them against the observed population in the SMC, LMC, and Milky Way. We find that the absence of wider WR binaries in the SMC, and potentially in the LMC, can be explained by stable, Case-B mass transfer only partially stripping the donor star, combined with WR winds at low metallicity being insufficiently strong to strip the remaining envelope. As a result, the long-period peak from Case-B mass transfer, present at Zsun, disappears at low metallicity. We additionally find that stable mass transfer (SMT) produces a short-period peak through Case-A mass transfer (P~5-10 days) that closely matches observations across metallicity. Furthermore, SMT and non-interacting systems are the dominant formation channels of WR binaries at all metallicities, with their relative contribution showing no metallicity dependence. This result implies that the SMT channel has the same metallicity-dependence as isolated WR formation. At the same time, we find that common envelope evolution primarily produces short-period ($P<1$ day) WR binaries with black-hole companions.

AI.tldr: Using detailed binary evolution models from POSYDON across metallicities from 0.01 to 1 Z☉, this study characterizes WR binary populations and finds that the absence of wide WR binaries at low metallicity (SMC/LMC) arises because Case-B stable mass transfer only partially strips donors and WR winds are too weak to remove remaining envelopes at low Z. Case-A mass transfer produces a short-period peak (~5-10 days) matching observations, while stable mass transfer and non-interacting systems dominate WR binary formation with no metallicity dependence, and common envelope evolution yields ultra-short-period WR+black hole systems.
AI.motivation: Observations show contrasting period distributions of WR binaries across the SMC, LMC, and Milky Way—short-period preference in low-metallicity galaxies but longer-period systems in the Galaxy—yet the metallicity dependence of WR binary formation, especially period distribution, remains poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors employ detailed binary evolution models from POSYDON to simulate populations of WR binaries at five metallicities (0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.45, 1 Z☉), analyze resulting period distributions and formation channels, and compare against observed WR binary populations in the SMC, LMC, and Milky Way.
AI.result: The absence of wide WR binaries at low metallicity is explained by partial stripping during stable Case-B mass transfer combined with insufficiently strong WR winds at low Z to remove remaining envelopes. Case-A SMT produces a short-period peak (~5-10 days) matching observations across all metallicities. SMT and non-interacting systems dominate WR binary formation regardless of metallicity, implying SMT has the same metallicity dependence as isolated WR formation. Common envelope evolution primarily forms short-period (<1 day) WR binaries with BH companions.
AI.conclusion: The metallicity-dependent disappearance of long-period WR binaries in low-Z environments is naturally explained by insufficient wind stripping following partial mass transfer, while short-period systems from Case-A mass transfer persist across metallicities. The dominance of SMT and non-interacting channels, with metallicity-independent relative contributions, suggests a universal formation mechanism scaling with isolated WR formation.

title: Resolved Dust-Gas-Metallicity relations in nearby spiral galaxies
comment: 23 pages, 12 figures, 2 tables. Resubmitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Context: Understanding the interstellar medium (ISM) requires high-resolution, multi-component mapping to capture its complex physical structure. Nearby spiral galaxies, with their abundant and diverse ISM, provide an ideal laboratory for such a comprehensive analysis at sub-galactic scales. Aims: We investigate dust-to-gas (DGR) and dust-to-metal (DMR) ratios as a functions of gas-phase metallicity (Z), on spatial scales ranging from 0.6 to 2.3 kpc, in a sample of 10 nearby spiral galaxies, spanning more than an order of magnitude in stellar mass (9.7 \le \log(M_*/M_\odot) \leq 11.0), star formation rate (SFR, \sim 0.3--3 \, M_\odot \, \rm yr^{-1}) and metallicity ranging from 8.3 \lesssim 12 + \log( O/H) \lesssim 8.8. We explore how the DGR-Z and DMR-Z relations are shaped by the assumptions behind the CO-to-H_2 conversion factor (α_{CO}). Methods: We homogeneously combine maps of dust, atomic gas, molecular gas, and metallicity. Motivated by the diversity in L_{CO(1-0)}/SFR ratios and metallicity across our sample, we introduce a hybrid α_{CO} prescription to distinguish between CO-bright and CO-dark regimes. The derived DGR-Z and DMR-Z relations are compared with other global and resolved observational results, and with the predictions of dust and chemical evolution models. Results: Both DGR-Z and DMR-Z relations are dependent on the adopted α_{CO} prescription, and no single α_{CO} can reproduce the properties of the entire sample, motivating the use of a hybrid approach. The DGR increases with metallicity, spanning \sim 1 dex across the sampled range; while the DMR remains approximately constant at \log(\mathrm{DMR}) = -0.53 \pm 0.13, implying that \sim 30 \% of metals are locked into dust grains. This flat behavior indicates an evolved dust phase where efficient ISM grain growth drives a saturation regime balancing dust formation and destruction.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes dust-to-gas (DGR) and dust-to-metal (DMR) ratios as functions of gas-phase metallicity across 10 nearby spiral galaxies on ~0.6–2.3 kpc scales, finding that the derived relations depend on the assumed CO-to-H2 conversion factor (α_CO). Using a novel hybrid α_CO prescription that distinguishes CO-bright from CO-dark gas, the authors find DGR increases ~1 dex with metallicity while DMR remains roughly constant at log(DMR) = −0.53 ± 0.13 (~30% of metals locked in dust), indicating an evolved dust phase with efficient grain growth reaching a saturation regime.
AI.motivation: Understanding the complex physical structure of the interstellar medium requires high-resolution, multi-component mapping. Nearby spiral galaxies provide an ideal laboratory for examining how dust content scales with metallicity at sub-galactic scales, and how such scaling relations depend on assumptions about molecular gas tracing via the CO-to-H2 conversion factor.
AI.method: The authors homogeneously combine maps of dust, atomic gas, molecular gas, and metallicity for 10 nearby spiral galaxies spanning stellar masses from 9.7 to 11.0 in log(M_*/M_sun), SFR ~0.3–3 M_sun/yr, and metallicities from 8.3 to 8.8 (12+log(O/H)). Motivated by the diversity in L_CO/SFR ratios and metallicity, they introduce a hybrid α_CO prescription that distinguishes CO-bright and CO-dark regimes, and compare derived DGR-Z and DMR-Z relations with global and resolved observations and with dust/chemical evolution models.
AI.result: Both DGR-Z and DMR-Z relations depend on the adopted α_CO prescription, and no single α_CO value reproduces the entire sample, supporting a hybrid approach. DGR increases with metallicity over ~1 dex across the sampled range. DMR is approximately constant at log(DMR) = −0.53 ± 0.13, implying ~30% of metals are locked into dust grains.
AI.conclusion: The flat DMR behavior indicates an evolved dust phase where efficient interstellar medium grain growth drives a saturation regime that balances dust formation and destruction processes.

title: Membership Determination of 45 Open Clusters Beyond 3 kpc
comment: 14 pages, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Context. Open clusters (OCs) are fundamental tracers for studying the structure and chemical evolution of the Galactic disc. Reliable identification of cluster members, particularly at the faint end of the main sequence, remains challenging owing to severe field-star contamination and the declining photometric completeness for distant, obscured systems. Aims. We aim to identify and characterise distant OC candidates at heliocentric distances $d \gtrsim 3$ kpc using Gaia DR3 astrometry, with emphasis on improving the recovery of faint candidate members in highly contaminated stellar fields. Methods. We apply a probabilistic membership method based on Gaia DR3 proper motions and parallaxes. Candidate members are selected through combined astrometric criteria and refined via spatial filtering using radial density profiles, with photometric data serving as a consistency check. For clusters affected by significant extinction, near-infrared photometry from 2MASS is incorporated to compensate for the limitations of optical data. Results. We analyse a sample of 45 targets, comprising 30 previously reported OCs and 15 newly identified candidates, all located at $d \gtrsim 3$ kpc. The method yields more compact astrometric distributions and improves the recovery of faint candidate members in several systems. title: AGN-DB: A Unified Multi-Wavelength Database of Active Galactic Nuclei
comment: Submitted to ApJ. Comments and inputs from the community are very welcome!
summary: We present the Active Galactic Nuclei Database (AGN-DB), a comprehensive, multi-wavelength catalog compiled from more than 100 publicly available AGN catalogs and samples released by the end of 2025, spanning radio to $γ$-ray wavelengths. The database contains approximately 8.1 million unique sources, approximately 7.8 million of which remain after flagging stellar contaminants, and approximately 6.8 million of these are classified as AGN. Source cross-matching across catalogs is performed using Lyra, a Bayesian likelihood-ratio framework that jointly considers positional uncertainties, source densities, and photometric information to compute posterior match probabilities. The resulting catalog provides astrometric coordinates, redshifts, photometry, and classifications for each unique source. All multi-catalog provenance is preserved. For every property, we store the full array of values and originating catalog identifiers, enabling multi-epoch and multi-survey analyses. In this paper, we describe the AGN-DB pipeline, including the cross-matching methodology, and present the statistical properties of the v1.0 catalog. AGN-DB is designed to enable population studies, spectral energy distribution modeling, AGN classification, and variability analyses at an unprecedented scale. Its pipeline is designed to facilitate the integration of new catalogs, allowing AGN-DB to be updated regularly, with releases planned at least annually.

AI.method: Compilation of AGN data from over 100 public catalogs and samples (radio to gamma-ray), followed by cross-matching using Lyra—a Bayesian likelihood-ratio framework that incorporates positional uncertainties, source densities, and photometric information to compute posterior match probabilities. Stellar contaminants are flagged, and all provenance, full property arrays, and originating catalog identifiers are preserved.

title: Recovering Ionizing Photon Escape and Galaxy Scaling Relations in the LzLCS via Si II and C II Absorption Lines and Mock Spectra from a Radiation-Hydrodynamic Simulation
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures
summary: In this work, we use a radiation-hydrodynamic simulation of a single $\sim10^9M_{\odot}$ virtual galaxy to study Si II and C II line profiles seen in stacked HST/COS spectra of 58 galaxies from the LzLCS+ sample. We compare stacks across three mass bins ($M_{\star} \leq 10^8M_{\odot}$, $10^8$-$10^9M_{\odot}$, and $M_{\star} \geq 10^9M_{\odot}$) and three stacking methods (mean, median, and weighted average) to a library of 22,500 mock spectra. We investigate whether the simulation can accurately mimic real gas features, reveal clear trends with galaxy properties, and provide indirect estimates of the ionizing escape fraction ($f_{\rm esc}$). We find reasonable agreement between simulated and observed profiles ($χ^2 < 1$) across all mass regimes. Notably, extracting line properties such as EW and $R_f$ from best-fit mock profiles provides a robust alternative to direct empirical trends, particularly in the low-S/N regime where noise frequently biases results. The simulation-based LIS features, although derived from a single virtual object, exhibit clear correlations with $M_{\star}$, SFR, and $f_{\rm esc}$, mirroring established empirical scaling relations. We find that the best-matching mock spectra predominantly originate from simulation time steps corresponding to peak UV luminosity and intense starburst phases, suggesting that these active periods generate the ISM diversity observed in star-forming galaxies. Finally, simulation-based estimates ($f_{\rm esc}^{\rm virtual}$) reproduce the observed mass-dependent trends in $f_{\rm esc}$ and are in close agreement with the average $f_{\rm esc}$ of the generated stacks. This simulation-based framework establishes a relevant methodology for interpreting spectroscopic observations, including inferring $f_{\rm esc}$ and characterizing physical scaling relations, in high-redshift galaxies from the Epoch of Reionization.

AI.method: The study simulates Si II and C II line profiles using a radiation-hydrodynamic simulation of a single ~10^9 M_sun virtual galaxy. It compares stacked HST/COS spectra of 58 galaxies from LzLCS+ across three mass bins and three stacking methods (mean, median, weighted average) against a library of 22,500 mock spectra, evaluating agreement via χ² and extracting line properties (EW, R_f) from best-fit mocks.

AI.conclusion: The simulation-based framework provides a robust methodology for interpreting spectroscopic observations and inferring f_esc and physical scaling relations in high-redshift Epoch of Reionization galaxies, even where direct empirical trends may be biased by low signal-to-noise.

title: Widespread Inflows Reveal Baryonic Cycling in Star-forming and Quiescent Galaxies
comment: 73 pages, 25 Figures (5 Main + 8 Extended Data + 12 Supplementary), submitted on 6th March 2026
summary: Cool-gas inflows, required to sustain star formation, have been fundamental in simulations yet remained observationally elusive. Using DESI spectroscopy of ~30,000 galaxies, we identify coherent inflowing gas (~100 km/s) in 20-50% of the sample, yielding a population-level census of gas flows. We uncover a striking inversion: inflows are detected in quiescent galaxies, whereas star-forming systems are dominated by gravitationally bound outflows. At fixed age, galaxies with inflows, outflows, or no/weak flows share similar masses, environments, and structures, indicating that these properties do not differentiate flow states. Instead, gas-flow state is linked to stellar population age and recent evolutionary history, consistent with age-dependent gas flows in two regimes. In some star-forming galaxies, elevated star formation surface densities drive outflows that recycle on ~0.5 Gyr timescales, consistent with a galactic fountain. In quiescent systems, low-level ``drizzling'' inflows persist, consistent with slowly cooling enriched halo gas and weak radio-mode nuclear activity. Broad gas-phase metallicity distributions---and absence of a pristine dilution signature---indicate that detected inflows are predominantly recycled or enriched. Detectability is modulated by dust, ionization, and geometry: in star-forming disks, inflowing gas lies near the disk plane and is obscured or ionized, while outflow hosts exhibit higher dust and metal content. As star formation declines, cold-outflow signatures weaken, and recycled or slowly cooling gas is more readily detected as inflow. Post-starburst galaxies provide snapshots of this transition. Our results resolve the scarcity of observed inflows, provide evidence for widespread gas accretion and recycling in present day galaxies, and establish an observational framework linking gas flows to star formation, chemical evolution, and galaxy structure.

Inflows are predominantly recycled or enriched gas, and detectability is modulated by dust, ionization, and geometry.

The scarcity of observed inflows has been a persistent puzzle, and this work aims to provide the first population-level census of gas flows using a large spectroscopic sample.

It compares flow states against galaxy properties (mass, environment, structure, stellar age, evolutionary history) and uses gas-phase metallicity distributions to test whether inflows are pristine or enriched/recycled.

Flow state does not correlate with mass, environment, or structure at fixed age, but instead links to stellar population age and recent evolutionary history. Two regimes emerge: star-forming galaxies exhibit galactic-fountain outflows recycling on ~0.5 Gyr timescales, while quiescent systems show low-level "drizzling" inflows consistent with slowly cooling halo gas and weak radio-mode AGN activity. title: H I Absorbers as Beacons of Hidden Structure at $z \sim 3$: Multi-Component, Metal-Rich Absorption System near a Protocluster
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 17 pages, 19 figures
summary: H I gas traces the large-scale structure and provides the primary fuel for star formation. High-$z$ protoclusters are ideal laboratories to study how H I gas is accreted and consumed during the formation of the most massive structures in the Universe. However, much remains unknown about the distribution and physical state of their H I gas. We examine a rare configuration in which a protocluster candidate is located in front of a quasar at $z=3.09$. Our spectroscopic campaign confirms a protocluster at $z=3.079$: however, no corresponding strong H I absorption is found in the background quasar spectrum. Instead, we serendipitously discover a prominent H I absorption feature at $z\sim 3.01$, offset by $\sim 60$ cMpc from the centre of the protocluster. Spanning an exceptionally broad velocity range of $\sim 2000$ km s$^{-1}$ ($\sim 40$ cMpc), this absorption is decoupled from the confirmed member galaxies. Detailed kinematic modelling reveals this absorption comprises five distinct components rather than a single cloud. Moreover, one of these components exhibits a super-solar metallicity ($[\mathrm{O/H}] = +1.19^{+0.91}_{-0.78}$). We propose two physical scenarios for this unique system: (1) an additional, hidden massive protocluster along the line of sight, and/or (2) metal-rich outflows and metal-poor inflows driven by a single massive galaxy. The discovery highlights that while protoclusters are not universally associated with strong H I absorption, targeting the strong H I absorbers may serve as a beacon for uncovering massive, metal-rich protoclusters or complex gas kinematics in the early Universe.

AI.tldr: A protocluster candidate at z=3.079 is confirmed in front of a quasar, but no associated strong HI absorption is found. Instead, prominent HI absorption at z~3.01, ~60 cMpc from the protocluster center, spanning ~2000 km/s is discovered with five distinct components, one showing super-solar metallicity. Two scenarios are proposed: a hidden massive protocluster or outflows/inflows from a massive galaxy.
AI.motivation: Understanding HI gas distribution and physical state in high-redshift protoclusters is critical for understanding how large-scale structures form and accrete fuel for star formation, yet this remains largely unknown.
AI.method: Spectroscopic observations of a protocluster candidate in front of a quasar at z=3.09, combined with kinematic modeling of HI absorption features detected in the background quasar spectrum.
AI.result: Confirms a protocluster at z=3.079 with no associated strong HI absorption; serendipitously discovers a broad (~2000 km/s) HI absorption feature at z~3.01 offset by ~60 cMpc, comprised of five distinct kinematic components, one exhibiting super-solar metallicity [O/H]=+1.19.
AI.conclusion: Protoclusters are not universally associated with strong HI absorption, but strong HI absorbers may be beacons for massive, metal-rich protoclusters or complex gas kinematics such as outflows/inflows in the early Universe.

title: Extending the Stellar-to-Halo Mass Relation to Dwarf Galaxies with DESI DR1
comment: 23 pages (+4 pages of appendices), 11 figures. Comments are welcome!
summary: Constraining the dark matter halos of the smallest galaxies offers fundamental insights into the nature of dark matter and stellar feedback. Using the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Data Release 1, we infer the stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR) down to the dwarf scale ($M_\star < 10^9\,M_\odot$), without extrapolation from the higher mass range. Leveraging the unprecedented depth of the DESI Bright Galaxy Survey at $0.01 < z < 0.2$, we construct 12 samples spanning nearly four orders of magnitude in stellar mass, and measure their projected clustering $w_p$, galaxy-galaxy lensing $ΔΣ$, as well as a novel observable: satellite occupation number $N_{\rm sat}$. The addition of $N_{\rm sat}$ enables robust subtraction of satellite contributions to both $w_p$ and $ΔΣ$ across the 12 individual halo occupation distribution analyses, yielding an average halo-to-stellar mass relation (HSMR) of $\log \langle M_h(M_\star) \rangle = 12.06 + 0.58\log(M_\star/10^{11}) + (M_\star/10^{11})^{0.73}$. Combining this HSMR with an observed stellar mass function, we constrain the SHMR across five orders of magnitude in halo mass, with the power-law slope steepening from $0.32 \pm 0.06$ above the Milky Way mass to $2.08 \pm 0.21$ in the dwarf regime. Interestingly, the scatter about the SHMR grows from $0.17 \pm 0.02$ dex at Milky Way-like scales to $0.68_{-0.33}^{+0.21}$ dex for systems comparable to the Large Magellanic Cloud, suggesting that smaller galaxies follow increasingly diverse evolutionary paths. Our work highlights the power of DESI in probing the galaxy-halo connection within the dwarf regime, offering an exciting avenue to bridge the gap between large-scale and near-field cosmologies in the future.

By measuring projected clustering, galaxy-galaxy lensing, and a new satellite occupation observable across 12 stellar mass samples, they derive an average halo-to-stellar mass relation and show the SHMR power-law slope steepens from 0.32 above Milky Way mass to 2.08 in the dwarf regime, with scatter growing from 0.17 to 0.68 dex, indicating increasingly diverse evolutionary paths for smaller galaxies.

title: Hint of bimodal Mg-Al anticorrelation in the metal-poor Globular Cluster NGC 4372
comment: 11 pages, 12 figures
summary: We present a detailed chemical abundance analysis of seven red giant branch stars in the very metal-poor globular cluster NGC~4372, based on high-resolution UVES spectra. Our study aims to characterize the chemical evolution of NGC~4372 and investigate the presence of multiple populations. We derived abundances for 17 elements, including light, iron-peak, $α$, and heavy elements, using both equivalent width and spectral synthesis methods. We find a mean cluster metallicity of [Fe/H]=$-$2.36 $\pm$ 0.03 dex, with no evidence of an intrinsic iron spread. The cluster exhibits a typical $α$-enhancement of [$α$/Fe]= 0.33 $\pm$ 0.05 dex and a well defined Na-O anticorrelation, confirming that NGC 4372 hosts at least two distinct stellar populations. Furthermore, the measured ratio of [Ba/Eu] =$-0.47 \pm 0.04$ indicates that the synthesis of heavy elements was dominated by $r$-process, consistent with other very metal-poor environments. We also identify a potential bimodal Mg-Al anticorrelation, which aligns with the patterns observed in GCs of similar mass and metallicity. These results reinforce the status of NGC 4372 as a cornerstone for understanding the early chemical enrichment of the Galactic Halo.

The cluster has a mean metallicity of [Fe/H]=-2.36±0.03, exhibits typical α-enhancement, shows a Na-O anticorrelation confirming at least two stellar populations, and its heavy element ratios ([Ba/Eu]=-0.47) indicate r-process dominance.
AI.motivation: To characterize the chemical evolution of the very metal-poor globular cluster NGC 4372 and investigate the presence of multiple stellar populations, thereby contributing to understanding the early chemical enrichment of the Galactic Halo.
AI.method: High-resolution UVES spectra were obtained for seven red giant branch stars. Chemical abundances for 17 elements (light, iron-peak, α, and heavy elements) were derived using both equivalent width and spectral synthesis methods.
