title: Linking orbital history to the quenching of isolated dwarf galaxies
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures, submitted to OJAp, comments welcome
summary: Recent discoveries of isolated dwarf galaxies (${M}_{\star}\sim 10^{7-9}~{\rm M}_{\odot}$) with no signs of ongoing star formation have challenged the prevailing notion that these solitary systems are exclusively star-forming. Investigating the origins of isolated quenched dwarfs provides important clues into the dominant processes driving galaxy quenching as a function of environment and stellar mass. In this study, we identify central dwarf galaxies in the Illustris-TNG50 cosmological simulation with ${M}_{\star} \sim 10^{7-9}~{\rm M}_{\odot}$, evaluate their star formation and orbital histories, and investigate how their dark matter halo properties correlate with quenching and interactions with massive neighbors. We find that $R_{\rm{peri}}$, defined as the closest separation ever attained between a central dwarf and a galaxy more massive than ${M}_{\star}> 10^{10}~{\rm M}_{\odot}$, is a reliable metric for inferring the star formation history of central dwarfs in TNG50. We also show that isolated quenched dwarf galaxies separate into backsplash and non-backsplash subpopulations as a function of $R_{\rm{peri}}$, and that non-backsplash galaxies are consistent with being quenched by cosmic web stripping or internal feedback mechanisms. Furthermore, we find that $R_{\rm{peri}}$ correlates strongly with dark matter halo mass and star formation proxies based on halo maximum circular velocity, which are commonly used in empirical galaxy-halo connection models. These predictions can be tested with data from upcoming deep and wide surveys (e.g., Rubin LSST and Roman) that are anticipated to significantly increase the cosmic census of dwarf galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using the Illustris-TNG50 cosmological simulation, this study identifies central dwarf galaxies ($M_\star \sim 10^{7-9} M_\odot$), finds that the closest-approach distance ($R_{\rm peri}$) to a massive neighbor ($>10^{10} M_\odot$) reliably predicts star formation history, and shows isolated quenched dwarfs split into backsplash and non-backsplash populations with distinct quenching mechanisms. $R_{\rm peri}$ also correlates with dark matter halo mass and maximum circular velocity proxies, providing testable predictions for upcoming surveys like Rubin LSST and Roman.
AI.motivation: Recent observations of isolated dwarf galaxies with no ongoing star formation challenge the assumption that solitary low-mass galaxies are exclusively star-forming. Understanding the origins of these isolated quenched dwarfs is key to identifying the dominant quenching processes as a function of environment and stellar mass.
AI.method: Central dwarf galaxies ($M_\star \sim 10^{7-9} M_\odot$) are identified in the Illustris-TNG50 cosmological simulation. Their star formation and orbital histories are evaluated, and correlations between dark matter halo properties, quenching, and interactions with massive neighbors are investigated. The metric $R_{\rm peri}$ (closest ever separation to a galaxy with $M_\star > 10^{10} M_\odot$) is used to classify and characterize quenched dwarfs.
AI.result: $R_{\rm peri}$ is a reliable predictor of central dwarf star formation history in TNG50. Isolated quenched dwarfs separate into backsplash and non-backsplash subpopulations based on $R_{\rm peri}$. Non-backsplash dwarfs are consistent with quenching via cosmic web stripping or internal feedback. $R_{\rm peri}$ correlates strongly with dark matter halo mass and with star formation proxies based on halo maximum circular velocity.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish $R_{\rm peri}$ as a key metric linking orbital history to quenching in isolated dwarf galaxies, and provide predictions testable with data from upcoming deep and wide surveys (e.g., Rubin LSST and Roman) that will greatly expand the dwarf galaxy census.

title: KKR 18: A Late Arrival Galaxy?
comment: 12 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: KKR 18 is a dwarf irregular galaxy in the Local Void at a distance of 9.46 Mpc. It is gas rich and was experiencing vigorous star formation 20 - 100 Myr ago. Its metallicity is 4% of Solar from an emission spectrum, qualifying is as extremely metal poor (XMP). Its most remarkable characteristic is an extremely deficient Red Giant Branch. This feature is shared with a small number of other dwarf galaxies and it is inferred that they lack ancient stellar components. It is suggested that these are late arrival galaxies (LAG).

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes KKR 18, a dwarf irregular galaxy in the Local Void at 9.46 Mpc, which is gas-rich, had vigorous star formation 20-100 Myr ago, and has an extremely low metallicity of 4% Solar (XMP). Its most striking feature is a highly deficient Red Giant Branch, implying a lack of ancient stellar components — a characteristic shared with a few other dwarf galaxies, leading to the suggestion that such galaxies may be late arrival galaxies (LAG).
AI.motivation: To understand the nature and implications of KKR 18's remarkably deficient Red Giant Branch, which suggests it lacks ancient stellar components, and to explore the hypothesis that such systems may be late arrival galaxies in their environment.
AI.method: The study examines KKR 18, a dwarf irregular galaxy in the Local Void at a distance of 9.46 Mpc, using its gas content, star formation history (vigorous 20-100 Myr ago), and low metallicity (4% Solar, making it extremely metal poor) to characterize its properties, with particular focus on its extremely deficient Red Giant Branch.
AI.result: KKR 18 is an extremely metal-poor, gas-rich dwarf irregular galaxy with recent vigorous star formation. Its extremely deficient Red Giant Branch implies a lack of ancient stellar populations, a feature shared with a small number of other dwarf galaxies.
AI.conclusion: It is suggested that dwarf galaxies like KKR 18 exhibiting deficient Red Giant Branches (and therefore lacking ancient stellar components) may be late arrival galaxies (LAG), representing a distinct class of systems that arrived relatively recently to their current environment.

title: Star Formation Evolution in Galaxy Pairs: Constraints from Morphological Disturbances and Recent Star Formation Histories
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures; accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Galaxy interactions can enhance star formation, but how star formation evolves during galaxy interactions remains poorly constrained by observations. We combine pair separation, morphological disturbance, and recent star formation history to study this evolution. We measure morphological disturbance with the shape asymmetry parameter ($A_{\rm shape}$) using deep images from the DESI Legacy Surveys, and use Galaxy Zoo DESI classifications as an independent test. We infer recent star formation histories by comparing SFR and $\mathrm{EW}(\mathrm{H}α)$, which trace current star formation, with $\mathrm{EW}(\mathrm{H}δ_A)$ and $D_n4000$, which are sensitive to stellar populations formed over longer timescales. At small projected separations, strongly disturbed galaxies show the strongest enhancements in SFR and $\mathrm{EW}(\mathrm{H}α)$, indicating that close encounters trigger strong star formation. At intermediate separations ($d_{\rm p}\sim100\,\mathrm{kpc}$), their current star formation is only moderately enhanced, but their $\mathrm{EW}(\mathrm{H}δ_A)$ enhancement is the strongest. This indicates a larger contribution from intermediate-age stars formed during stronger star formation in the past $\sim0.1$--$1\,\mathrm{Gyr}$. The TNG100 analysis shows that this pattern results from rapid changes in SFR around close passage. SFR rises sharply during the encounter and declines as the galaxies move apart, while tidal disturbances remain visible. As short-lived massive stars disappear and intermediate-age A-type stars begin to dominate the spectrum, the $\mathrm{EW}(\mathrm{H}δ_A)$ enhancement peaks later than the SFR enhancement. Our results provide important observational evidence for the evolution of SFR along the merger sequence.

AI.tldr: This paper combines pair separation, morphological disturbance (via shape asymmetry from DESI Legacy Surveys), and recent star formation history (using SFR, EW(Hα), EW(Hδ_A), and D_n4000) to trace how star formation evolves during galaxy interactions and mergers.
AI.motivation: How star formation evolves during galaxy interactions remains poorly constrained by observations, despite the known ability of interactions to enhance star formation.
AI.method: The authors use shape asymmetry (A_shape) from DESI Legacy Surveys for morphological disturbance (validated with Galaxy Zoo DESI), and compare instantaneous star formation tracers (SFR, EW(Hα)) with longer-timescale tracers (EW(Hδ_A), D_n4000) across different pair separations. TNG100 simulations are used to interpret the observed patterns.
AI.result: Strongly disturbed galaxies at small separations show the strongest SFR and EW(Hα) enhancements. At intermediate separations (~100 kpc), current star formation is only moderately enhanced, but EW(Hδ_A) enhancement peaks, indicating past enhanced star formation 0.1–1 Gyr ago. TNG100 shows SFR rises sharply during close passage then declines as galaxies separate, while EW(Hδ_A) peaks later as short-lived massive stars fade and intermediate-age A-type stars dominate.
AI.conclusion: The results provide important observational evidence for the evolutionary sequence of star formation enhancement during galaxy mergers, showing a time-delay between the peak of current star formation and the peak of signatures from intermediate-age stellar populations.

title: Quantifying collision-driven mass loss in supermassive star formation: the role of stellar structure and accretion
summary: Observations of high-redshift galaxies with JWST have renewed interest in scenarios where supermassive stars form via runaway stellar collisions in dense clusters, yet the impact of collision-driven mass loss on their growth remains uncertain. In this work, we perform a post-processing analysis of 3D hydrodynamical simulations of the formation of a supermassive star, applying an analytic mass-loss prescription to stellar collisions while exploring different assumptions for the internal stellar structure. We consider a polytropic main-sequence model, a semi-analytic accreting protostar model, and structures derived from stellar evolution calculations. We find that the cumulative mass-loss fraction depends sensitively on the adopted stellar structure, ranging from $\lesssim 10-25\%$ for more compact configurations to $\gtrsim 30-40\%$ for more extended protostellar models. The importance of mass loss further depends on the dynamical state of the system, including the ratio of stellar velocity dispersion to the stellar surface escape velocity. We find significant uncertainty depending on the prescription used. As a result, collision-driven mass loss could significantly limit the growth of the central object, at least in some cases. Overall, our results indicate that uncertainties in the internal structure of rapidly accreting protostars represent a major source of systematic uncertainty and must be better constrained to robustly assess the viability of runaway-collision pathways for forming massive black hole seeds.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how collision-driven mass loss affects the growth of supermassive stars via runaway stellar collisions, finding that mass loss depends sensitively on assumed internal stellar structure (ranging from ~10-25% for compact configurations to ~30-40% for extended protostellar models), introducing significant systematic uncertainty in assessing the viability of this massive black hole seed formation pathway.
AI.motivation: JWST observations of high-redshift galaxies have renewed interest in supermassive star formation via runaway stellar collisions in dense clusters, but the impact of collision-driven mass loss on stellar growth is poorly understood and remains a key source of uncertainty.
AI.method: Post-processing analysis of 3D hydrodynamical simulations of supermassive star formation, applying an analytic mass-loss prescription to stellar collisions while testing different assumptions for internal stellar structure, including polytropic main-sequence models, semi-analytic accreting protostar models, and structures from stellar evolution calculations.
AI.result: Cumulative mass-loss fraction varies strongly with adopted structure (less than 10-25% for compact configurations to greater than 30-40% for extended protostellar models). Mass-loss importance also depends on the dynamical state, notably the ratio of stellar velocity dispersion to surface escape velocity. Significant prescription-dependent uncertainty is found, and collision-driven mass loss may substantially limit central object growth in some cases.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainties in the internal structure of rapidly accreting protostars are a major source of systematic uncertainty in collision-driven growth scenarios, and must be better constrained to robustly evaluate runaway-collision pathways for forming massive black hole seeds.

title: Rubin J122659.4+090236: An Extremely Low Surface Brightness Galaxy Candidate Discovered in the Rubin LSST Early Data Preview 2
comment: 16 pages (including appendices), 9 figures, 4 tables
summary: We report the serendipitous discovery of an exceptionally low surface brightness galaxy (LSBG) candidate, Rubin J122659.4+090236, in Rubin Observatory imaging of the interacting NGC 4410 system, identified in the Cosmic Treasure Chest public release. 2D Sérsic modelling of the Rubin g, r, and i images reveals a nearly round system with a shallow profile (n ~ 0.4), an effective radius of R_e ~ 6'', and central surface brightnesses of $μ_{0,g}=27.52\pm0.04$, $μ_{0,r}=27.62\pm0.07$, and $μ_{0,i}=27.04\pm0.08$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$. EAZY photo-z fitting favours an intermediate-z solution at z~0.3, while a low-redshift solution at z~0.028, consistent with the NGC 4410 system, is also permitted by a restricted EAZY fit over 0<z<0.1 without imposing a redshift prior. These alternatives imply substantially different physical interpretations, ranging from a diffuse dwarf-like system to an exceptionally extended background LSBG. This discovery demonstrates Rubin's sensitivity to extremely diffuse galaxies and highlights the potential of the LSST survey to uncover large samples of such elusive systems across wide areas, enabling systematic studies of the LSBG population and its role in galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: A serendipitously discovered exceptionally low surface brightness galaxy candidate, Rubin J122659.4+090236, was found in Rubin Observatory imaging of the interacting NGC 4410 system. Sérsic modelling reveals a nearly round, shallow-profile system with very low central surface brightnesses. Photo-z fitting yields two viable redshift solutions (z~0.3 or z~0.028), implying different physical interpretations from a diffuse dwarf to an extended background LSBG, highlighting Rubin/LSST's capability to detect extremely diffuse galaxies.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate Rubin Observatory's sensitivity to exceptionally diffuse low surface brightness galaxies and to highlight LSST's potential for discovering large samples of such elusive systems for systematic population studies.
AI.method: The discovery was serendipitous in Rubin imaging of the NGC 4410 system (Cosmic Treasure Chest public release). 2D Sérsic modelling was applied to Rubin g, r, and i-band images, and EAZY photometric redshift fitting was performed, including a restricted fit over 0<z<0.1 without imposing a redshift prior.
AI.result: The galaxy is nearly round with a shallow Sérsic index n~0.4, an effective radius of R_e~6'', and central surface brightnesses of ~27.0-27.6 mag arcsec^-2 in g, r, and i. EAZY favours z~0.3, but a restricted fit permits z~0.028 consistent with the NGC 4410 system.
AI.conclusion: The two redshift scenarios imply conflicting physical interpretations (diffuse dwarf-like system vs. exceptionally extended background LSBG), and the discovery underscores Rubin/LSST's sensitivity to extremely diffuse galaxies and its potential to enable systematic studies of the LSBG population and its role in galaxy evolution.

title: Corona Australis 151: an extremely young protostar
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A Letters
summary:
Context. Prestellar cores are the birthplace of stars and planetary systems, but they are short-lived objects, since the initial stages of dense core evolution, collapse, and the formation of a protostellar seed are fast. In an effort to build a catalogue of bona-fide prestellar cores in the Solar neighbourhood, we used APEX observations to identify dynamically evolved cores among dense cores observed with Herschel. One of them, Corona Australis 151, stood out because of its centrally peaked structure, with densities above 1e7cm-3 in the central 500-1000 au, and high deuteration levels (N2D+/N2H+~0.5), suggestive of an evolved, prestellar stage.
  Aims. Corona Australis 151 appears to be an evolved prestellar core, but the presence of broad wings in some of the detected lines and a tentative 70micron detection with Herschel partially challenges its prestellar stage. We intend to assess its evolutionary stage.
  Methods. We analyse new ALMA data of the continuum emission and of several line tracers (including typical outflow tracers) at a resolution of~150-200au, tracing the envelope.
  Results. We unveil the presence of a compact and young outflow (projected dynamical age:~500yr), traced by SiO, CO, and H2CO emission. The continuum emission traces an envelope structure of size~1000 au and mass 0.33M_sun(assuming Tdust=20 K).
  Conclusions. Corona Australis 151 is an extremely young protostar, possibly one of the youngest known in the Solar neighbourhood, and hence a new laboratory to study the chemical and dynamical evolution at the dawn of star formation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents ALMA observations of Corona Australis 151, a previously classified prestellar core, revealing it to be an extremely young protostar with a compact outflow (projected dynamical age ~500 yr) and an envelope of ~1000 au and 0.33 M_sun, making it one of the youngest known protostars in the Solar neighbourhood.
AI.motivation: Prestellar cores are short-lived and important for understanding star formation. Corona Australis 151 showed signs of an evolved prestellar core (high central densities and deuteration), but broad line wings and a tentative 70-micron detection challenged this classification, motivating a determination of its true evolutionary stage.
AI.method: New ALMA observations at ~150-200 au resolution were used to analyse continuum emission and several line tracers (including outflow tracers such as SiO, CO, and H2CO) to trace the envelope and assess the core's evolutionary status.
AI.result: A compact, young outflow (projected dynamical age ~500 yr) was detected via SiO, CO, and H2CO emission. The continuum emission traces an envelope of ~1000 au size and 0.33 M_sun mass (assuming Tdust = 20 K).
AI.conclusion: Corona Australis 151 is not a prestellar core but an extremely young protostar, potentially one of the youngest known in the Solar neighbourhood, providing a unique laboratory for studying the chemical and dynamical evolution at the onset of star formation.

title: PPN--spin degeneracies in mock S62-like stellar-orbit inference
comment: 21 pages, 15 figures
summary: We investigate the degeneracies between black hole (BH) spin effects and parametrized post-Newtonian (PPN) parameters in the relativistic orbital dynamics of S2-like and S62-like stars orbiting Sagittarius A$^{\ast}$. Using a 1PN+SO Hamiltonian framework and synthetic astrometric and radial velocity datasets, we perform Bayesian parameter inference. For current baseline observational precisions, the dominant relativistic observable--the Schwarzschild periapsis advance--allows the recovery of the effective precession parameter $Υ$, while leaving the individual PPN parameters $γ$ and $β$ degenerate. Assuming microarcsecond-level astrometric precision, the spin-induced Lense-Thirring signal becomes partially detectable; fixing the PPN sector to General Relativity allows the BH spin magnitude to be constrained to an uncertainty of $\sim10^{-2}$. However, simultaneously varying PPN and spin parameters reveals a strong, approximately linear covariance between $Υ$ and the dimensionless spin parameter $χ$. To overcome this limitation, we demonstrate that joint multi-star inference can disentangle the degeneracy by combining a wider-orbit star, which constrains the dominant 1PN sector, with a compact relativistic orbit that is sensitive to Lense-Thirring frame dragging.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates degeneracies between black hole spin effects and parametrized post-Newtonian (PPN) parameters in the orbital dynamics of S2-like and S62-like stars around Sagittarius A*. Using a 1PN+SO Hamiltonian framework and Bayesian inference on synthetic data, the authors find that the Schwarzschild periapsis advance constrains the effective precession parameter but leaves individual PPN parameters degenerate. At microarcsecond precision, Lense-Thirring spin effects become partially detectable, but a strong linear covariance exists between the precession parameter and spin when varied simultaneously. Joint multi-star inference—combining a wider-orbit star with a compact relativistic orbit—can disentangle this degeneracy.
AI.motivation: To understand whether gravitational tests using stellar orbits around Sagittarius A* can separate general relativistic spin effects (Lense-Thirring) from potential deviations in the PPN parameters, particularly as observational precision improves toward microarcsecond levels.
AI.method: The study employs a 1PN+Spin-Orbit (SO) Hamiltonian framework to model the orbital dynamics of S2-like and S62-like stars. Synthetic astrometric and radial velocity datasets are generated and analyzed via Bayesian parameter inference to probe degeneracies between PPN parameters (γ, β, and effective precession parameter Υ) and the BH spin parameter χ.
AI.result: At current observational precisions, only the effective precession parameter Υ can be recovered (individual γ and β remain degenerate). With microarcsecond astrometry, the Lense-Thirring signal becomes partially detectable; fixing PPN sector to GR constrains spin to ~10^-2 uncertainty. However, simultaneous fitting reveals a strong approximately linear covariance between Υ and χ. Joint multi-star inference successfully breaks this degeneracy by pairing a wide-orbit star (constraining 1PN sector) with a compact orbit (sensitive to frame dragging).
AI.conclusion: Joint multi-star astrometric and spectroscopic monitoring of stellar orbits around Sagittarius A* can disentangle the covariance between PPN precession parameters and black hole spin, enabling cleaner tests of GR and more robust spin measurements, provided microarcsecond-level precision is achieved.

title: The dispersal law of young star clusters: free expansion -- A Gaia/eROSITA census of Orion and Sco--Cen
comment: Submitted to A&A. Comments are welcome
summary: We measure how young star clusters disperse over time in the two nearest star-forming complexes. Our sample comprises 44 \texttt{SigMA}-\textit{Gaia}-defined clusters in Orion and 31 in Sco--Cen, with isochronal ages of 2--25\,Myr. We extend each cluster's census with \textit{eROSITA}-selected young stars that share its parallax and motion and lie within the distance they could have traveled ballistically since birth. By 10--30\,Myr, about one in three former cluster stars lies outside the cluster's cataloged boundary. Across both complexes and the full age range, we find that (1) the half-member radius increases linearly with age, $\rfifty \simeq \sigbirth t$, (2) the velocity dispersion shows no measurable evolution, and (3) all studied clusters are unbound. These results support free expansion. Young clusters in Orion and Sco-Cen emerge unbound from their birth clouds and coast at their birth velocity dispersion without significant relaxation or a characteristic dispersal timescale. We further show that memberships defined by density contrast preferentially omit the fastest stars, making the same clusters appear to expand more slowly ($\propto t^{0.6}$), cool with age, and approach equilibrium.

AI.tldr: The authors analyze 75 young (2–25 Myr) star clusters across Orion and Sco–Cen using Gaia and eROSITA data, finding that clusters expand freely at a linear rate (half-member radius ∝ age), show no velocity dispersion evolution, and are all unbound. They conclude these clusters emerge unbound from birth clouds and coast ballistically, while density-contrast-based membership methods bias observations toward slower-expanding, apparently equilibrated clusters.
AI.motivation: To understand how young star clusters disperse over time and whether observed expansion behavior reflects true physical free expansion or is an artifact of membership selection methods.
AI.method: Analysis of 44 SigMA-Gaia clusters in Orion and 31 in Sco-Cen (2–25 Myr), extending member censuses with eROSITA-selected young stars that share parallax/motion and lie within ballistic travel distances since birth. They measure half-member radius growth, velocity dispersion evolution, and binding status.
AI.result: Half-member radius grows linearly with age (r50 ≈ σ_birth × t), velocity dispersion shows no measurable evolution, all clusters are unbound, and ~1 in 3 former cluster members lies outside cataloged boundaries by 10–30 Myr. Density-contrast-based membership definitions preferentially omit fast stars, making clusters appear to expand more slowly (t^0.6), cool, and reach equilibrium.
AI.conclusion: Young clusters in Orion and Sco–Cen emerge unbound from their birth clouds and expand freely at their birth velocity dispersion, with no significant relaxation or characteristic dispersal timescale. Apparent slower expansion and equilibration reported previously may result from selection biases in density-based membership methods.

title: Stellar Population and Dynamical Modeling of Galaxies with Kinematically Misaligned Components: Age and Metallicity of Structural Components
comment: 31 pages, 16 figures, 4 tables
summary: We present stellar population and orbit modeling of two galaxies with kinematically misaligned components, PGC 35706 and LEDA 2220522, extending previous Schwarzschild dynamical models. Using spatially resolved age and metallicity maps from NBursts full spectral fitting of MaNGA data with the E-MILES grid, we solve a regularized bounded linear inverse problem that assigns light-weighted SSP-equivalent age, metallicity, and mass-to-light ratio to orbital cells in the $(R,λ_z)$ plane. Component means and radial profiles use projected mass within the actual MaNGA field of view; profile segments with local component fractions below $1\%$ are treated as weakly constrained. In LEDA 2220522, the counter-rotating disk is younger than the co-rotating disk, $1.32\pm0.04$ versus $1.61\pm0.06$ Gyr, and more metal-rich, $[\mathrm{M/H}]=-0.450\pm0.043$ versus $-0.613\pm0.024$. Its rotation agrees with that of the H$α$ ionized gas, supporting late supply of chemically enriched retrograde gas without requiring multiple accretion episodes with alternating angular momentum. In PGC 35706, the counter-rotating disk contains $8.8\%$ of the mass in the observed field and is formally older than the co-rotating disk by $1.36\pm0.51$ Gyr and more metal-poor by $0.130\pm0.046$ dex. These differences are preliminary because the projected data provide limited support. Fifty Monte Carlo realizations confirm stability of the projected maps against statistical noise, but not uniqueness in individual phase-space cells. The stellar population and orbit approach is therefore applicable to MaNGA data when local projected component fractions and systematics from regularization and the dynamical model are explicitly considered.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Schwarzschild dynamical models of two galaxies (PGC 35706 and LEDA 2220522) with kinematically misaligned components by adding stellar population modeling. Using MaNGA data fitted with NBursts and the E-MILES grid, the authors solve a regularized linear inverse problem to assign light-weighted age, metallicity, and mass-to-light ratio to orbital cells in the (R, λ_z) plane. In LEDA 2220522, the counter-rotating disk is younger and more metal-rich than the co-rotating disk, consistent with late accretion of enriched retrograde gas. In PGC 35706, the counter-rotating disk is formally older and more metal-poor but with limited support. Monte Carlo simulations confirm stability of projected maps but not uniqueness in individual cells.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation and evolution of galaxies with kinematically misaligned components (e.g., counter-rotating disks) by combining stellar population information with orbital dynamics, extending previous Schwarzschild models that lacked spatially resolved age and metallicity constraints.
AI.method: Schwarzschild dynamical models extended with stellar population modeling: spatially resolved age and metallicity maps are obtained from NBursts full spectral fitting of MaNGA data using the E-MILES stellar population grid. A regularized bounded linear inverse problem assigns light-weighted SSP-equivalent age, metallicity, and mass-to-light ratio to orbital cells in the (R, λ_z) plane, with component means and radial profiles computed from projected mass within the MaNGA field of view.
AI.result: In LEDA 2220522, the counter-rotating disk is younger (1.32±0.04 vs 1.61±0.06 Gyr) and more metal-rich ([M/H]=-0.450±0.043 vs -0.613±0.024) than the co-rotating disk, and its rotation matches the Hα gas. In PGC 35706, the counter-rotating disk holds 8.8% of the field mass and appears older and more metal-poor, though with limited support. Fifty Monte Carlo realizations confirm projected-map stability against noise but not cell-by-cell uniqueness.
AI.conclusion: The coupled stellar population and orbit modeling approach is viable for MaNGA data provided local projected component fractions, regularization systematics, and dynamical model uncertainties are explicitly accounted for. The results support a late gas accretion scenario for LEDA 2220522 without needing multiple accretion episodes with alternating angular momentum, while the PGC 35706 finding is preliminary.

title: Rapid quenching and early gas depletion in the core of a galaxy protocluster at z=2.2
comment: 16 pages (of which 2 pages for Appendices), 9 Figures, 4 Tables. A&A in press
summary: Understanding how galaxy evolution is affected in forming high-z overdensities is a major open question in modern astrophysics. Here, we present the average properties of the quiescent galaxy population recently identified in the core of the Spiderweb protocluster at z = 2.16. By stacking observations from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST; F160W imaging and G141 grism spectroscopy), the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST; PaBeta narrowband imaging), and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA; 1.2 mm dust continuum imaging), we constrained their ensemble star formation history (SFH), residual dust-obscured star formation, and cold gas mass, respectively. The inferred average SFH indicates steady stellar mass growth, with progenitor SFRs consistent with those of massive Halpha emitters (HAEs) in the same structure. This is followed by rapid quenching, on average 500 Myr prior to observation. No significant age differences are found between active galactic nucleus (AGN) hosts and non-AGN systems. We find weak PaBeta emission for 80% of the sample, yet with dust-obscured star formation rates consistent with quiescence in all but one source (ID 443) excluded from the sample. Our galaxies remain individually and globally undetected in the dust continuum, yielding an average gas fraction fgas= Mmol/Mstar<7%, consistent with previously reported gas depletion trends with stellar mass observed in neighboring HAEs. We thus find the Spiderweb protocluster to host a sizable population of gas-depleted, massive quenched galaxies in its core, likely descending from main-sequence galaxy progenitors and building the first elements of the red sequence in this high-z forming cluster.

AI.tldr: The paper constrains the ensemble star formation history, dust-obscured star formation, and cold gas content of quiescent galaxies in the core of the Spiderweb protocluster at z=2.16 by stacking HST, JWST, and ALMA observations. The quiescent galaxies show steady mass growth followed by rapid quenching ~500 Myr before observation, are largely gas-depleted (fgas<7%), and lack significant age differences between AGN hosts and non-AGN systems.

AI.method: Stacking multi-wavelength observations from HST (F160W imaging and G141 grism spectroscopy), JWST (PaBeta narrowband imaging), and ALMA (1.2 mm dust continuum imaging) to constrain the average star formation history, residual dust-obscured star formation, and cold gas mass of the quiescent galaxy population.

No significant age differences found between AGN hosts and non-AGN systems. Galaxies remain undetected in dust continuum individually and globally, yielding an average gas fraction fgas<7%, consistent with gas depletion trends with stellar mass in neighboring HAEs.
AI.conclusion: The Spiderweb protocluster hosts a sizable population of gas-depleted, massive quenched galaxies in its core, likely descending from main-sequence galaxy progenitors and building the first elements of the red sequence in this high-redshift forming cluster.
